facts.label: Version relationships and conflicts
facts.text: - Periodic reports are separate, non-duplicate sources: each 10-Q covers a different quarter, and each release is a separate furnished exhibit for the same quarter as the 10-Q of the same date. None is a retained duplicate of another; none is collapsed. The later 10-Q restates balances as of the earlier fiscal year end (October 3, 2025) alongside current balances, so the 10-K and the Q3 10-Q both hold October 3, 2025 figures; downstream modules must cite the filing they use. - Credit Agreement versions: the Q2 10-Q describes the original agreement, a first amendment (February 22, 2024) and a second amendment (May 1, 2025) and states the second amendment raised the maximum leverage ratio from 4.50x to step-down levels (Q2 10-Q page:20). The Q3 10-Q states the schedule that currently applies (page:20). The amendments themselves are not supplied. The first amendment is listed as an exhibit (10-K page:152); the executed text is not in the pack. - Transformation plan cost estimate differs between sources by date, not by error: the 10-K subsequent events note estimates "range of $25 million to $30 million" (10-K page:147) and the Q3 10-Q estimates "range of $35 million to $40 million" (page:42). The later filing controls for current estimates; downstream modules must say which they use. - Net leverage definition: the Q3 10-Q describes the covenant term as including advances under any receivables facility (page:52), while the Q3 release defines Net Debt as principal debt, letters of credit and finance lease obligations less cash (release page:10). The release's printed Net Debt table lists no receivables facility line (release page:16). This is an unresolved definitional difference between a filing and a release; the filing and the executed agreement control. Effect: the reported ratio may not equal the covenant ratio, and any covenant-headroom statement must say so. It is not resolved here. - Management claims versus filings: release statements about outlook, savings and operating metrics are attributed management claims; the filings control reported figures.

facts.text: Three issues keep the view at medium confidence. First, the executed credit agreement is not in the pack, so the covenant definition is read from summaries, and those summaries define covenant indebtedness to include advances under any receivables facility (Q3 10-Q page:52) while the company's net debt table has no such line (release page:16); the sold receivables balance was 212.3 million at July 3, 2026. Second, the maximum leverage ratio steps down to 4.75x for the quarter ending October 2, 2026 and 4.50x from the first quarter of fiscal 2027 (Q3 10-Q page:20), so today's headroom is not permanent. Third, the receivables facility is scheduled to terminate on August 2, 2027 (Q3 10-Q page:50); because the sold balance is off balance sheet, its end would draw on liquidity. The credit read-through is a deleveraging credit with adequate near-term liquidity and no bank maturity before fiscal 2028, but with a covenant test that tightens, definition risk around receivables, a shrinking top line and an earnings recovery driven by cost reductions and pricing while revenue and volume still decline.

facts.label: Calculation steps
facts.text: - Principal debt reduction: 1,168,500 less 1,097,500 equals 71,000 (US$ thousands) between October 3, 2025 and July 3, 2026. - Total debt for the leverage chart: principal debt plus finance lease obligations. FY2025: 1,168,500 + 166,305 = 1,334,805. Q1: 1,161,500 + 162,738 = 1,324,238. Q2: 1,127,500 + 164,717 = 1,292,217. Q3: 1,097,500 + 159,723 = 1,257,223. - Net debt for the chart: total debt less cash. FY2025: 1,334,805 - 29,748 = 1,305,057. Q1: 1,324,238 - 41,547 = 1,282,691. Q2: 1,292,217 - 50,340 = 1,241,877. Q3: 1,257,223 - 57,659 = 1,199,564. - Trailing twelve month Adjusted EBITDA (company): 257,425; 246,606; 273,592; 290,437 (release page:16). Total debt / EBITDA: 1,334,805 / 257,425 = 5.185 (5.19); 1,324,238 / 246,606 = 5.370 (5.37); 1,292,217 / 273,592 = 4.723 (4.72); 1,257,223 / 290,437 = 4.329 (4.33). Net debt / EBITDA: 1,305,057 / 257,425 = 5.070 (5.07); 1,282,691 / 246,606 = 5.201 (5.20); 1,241,877 / 273,592 = 4.539 (4.54); 1,199,564 / 290,437 = 4.130 (4.13). - Trailing cash interest paid on principal debt (US$ millions, printed to one decimal): FY2025 93.6. Q1: 93.6 + 20.1 - 23.2 = 90.5 (Q1 10-Q page:15). Q2: 93.6 + 38.3 - 43.8 = 88.1 (Q2 10-Q page:16). Q3: 93.6 + 55.7 - 64.7 = 84.6 (Q3 10-Q page:16). - Interest cover: 257.425 / 93.6 = 2.750; 246.606 / 90.5 = 2.725; 273.592 / 88.1 = 3.105; 290.437 / 84.6 = 3.433. - Covenant-style interest cover, indicative only: the covenant is Adjusted EBITDA over consolidated interest expense, minimum 2.00x (Q3 10-Q page:52). The company does not print the ratio. Covenant Adjusted EBITDA over interest expense, net: Q3 LTM 294,037 / 87,717 = 3.352 (3.35x); FY2025 277,825 / 92,264 = 3.011 (3.01x). The agreement's definition of consolidated interest expense is not supplied, so these are not compliance figures. - Cover including receivables facility fees, mixed basis: securitization fees LTM 12,163 (release page:14). LTM Adjusted EBITDA adds these fees back, so charging them as a financing cost: 290.437 / (84.6 + 12.163) = 3.002 (3.00x). Cash interest is on a paid basis and the fees are on an expense basis. - EBITDA unadjusted: Q3 FY2026 11,046 + 3,298 + 20,118 + 33,272 = 67,734. Q3 FY2025: -676 + -73 + 22,495 + 34,856 = 56,602. 9M FY2026: 7,251 + 1,045 + 63,374 + 102,181 = 173,851. 9M FY2025: -27,674 + -5,727 + 67,921 + 107,674 = 142,194. FY2025: -40,223 + -4,083 + 92,264 + 143,017 = 190,975. LTM: -5,298 + 2,689 + 87,717 + 137,524 = 222,632. - Free cash flow: Q3 FY2026 64,935 - 17,955 = 46,980. Q3 FY2025 22,864 - 14,860 = 8,004. 9M FY2026 160,873 - 40,031 = 120,842. 9M FY2025 33,302 - 43,102 = -9,800. FY2025 64,229 - 58,460 = 5,769. LTM operating cash flow 64,229 + 160,873 - 33,302 = 191,800; LTM purchases 58,460 + 40,031 - 43,102 = 55,389; LTM free cash flow 191,800 - 55,389 = 136,411. facts.text: - Fiscal 2025 Adjusted EBITDA: the outlook tables in the Q2 and Q3 releases show fiscal 2025 actual Adjusted EBITDA of $272.6 million (Q3 release page:4), while the reconciliation shows 257,425 for the twelve months ended October 3, 2025 (release page:14). facts.label: Business and transaction view
facts.text: Vestis is a standalone, publicly listed provider of uniform rental and workplace supplies in the United States and Canada, created by the spin-off from Aramark on September 30, 2023. The sources disclose no sponsor, and no parent or borrower distinct from the listed registrant is named in them; they show no leveraged buyout, acquisition or dividend recapitalisation in the period examined. The one transaction that defines the capital structure is the separation itself: the company borrowed under a new senior secured credit agreement and transferred roughly 1,457 million (US$) of proceeds to Aramark (10-K page:112). Since then the only financing changes are a refinancing of one term loan in February 2024, a covenant amendment in May 2025 that traded relief for restrictions on dividends, buybacks and receivables facilities, and a receivables securitization put in place in August 2024.

facts.label: Business and transaction view
facts.text: The operating model gives good revenue visibility: recurring weekly rental service under multi-year contracts is 95% of revenue, more than 300,000 accounts and no meaningful concentration (the ten largest customers are under 10% of revenue). The countervailing evidence is that revenue is nonetheless contracting: the nine-month decline in revenue and the quarter's lower volume are explained in part by a deliberate exit of unprofitable business under the transformation plan, and fiscal 2025 revenue included the loss of a national account customer. The mechanism matters for creditors: a recurring base protects against sudden revenue loss, but contract exit costs are modest relative to a service-quality failure, and the business has a high fixed cost base of plants and routes, so volume decline compresses operating leverage unless cost is removed at the same pace. This is why the earlier financial handoff shows earnings recovery driven by cost reduction and pricing rather than volume.

facts.label: Business and transaction view
facts.text: The credit-relevant change is the transformation plan launched in the first quarter of fiscal 2026. Management targets annual cost savings of at least $75 million by the end of fiscal 2026 and has roughly $30 million realised through the third quarter (Q3 release page:2). These are management claims, not filed facts; the filed fact is that third-party consulting and severance costs have been incurred and that the estimated plan cost has been raised since the 10-K. Governance signals are mixed rather than adverse: no extraction-oriented behaviour is documented, dividends are suspended by the credit agreement amendment, but the principal financial officer role is filled on an interim basis and securities class actions allege misleading statements about pricing practices and outlook (allegations, not findings). Evidence quality is High for filed facts and Low for management claims on savings and market position.

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: The transaction history in the sources is the separation from Aramark and the financings around it; there is no sponsor transaction, acquisition or disposal of size, and no new debt issue in fiscal 2026 to the cutoff. On September 29, 2023 the company and certain subsidiaries entered into a senior secured credit agreement, and the separation was completed on September 30, 2023 by a distribution of Vestis shares to Aramark holders at one Vestis share for every two Aramark shares; the company used about 1,457 million of term loan proceeds to transfer cash to Aramark (10-K page:112, page:145). The agreement was amended on February 22, 2024 to refinance the original 800 million term loan A-1 with an 800 million term loan B-1 due February 2031, and on May 1, 2025 to raise the maximum net leverage ratio in stages, grant a one-time 15 million bad debt adjustment to covenant EBITDA, cap receivables facilities at 250 million and restrict dividends and share repurchases (10-K page:113, page:115). A three-year 250 million accounts receivable securitization was put in place on August 2, 2024 (10-K page:146). Use of proceeds on the securitization was repayment of part of the term loans (Q3 10-Q page:50). In fiscal 2026 the sources show only repayments of principal, with no new instrument. Liquidity effect and covenant terms are in the earlier financial handoff and are company-reported; the executed amendments are not supplied. The company also sold its equity stake in Aramark Uniform Services Japan Corporation in the first quarter of fiscal 2025 (Q3 10-Q page:15). Status of every item above: completed; none is draft or pending.

facts.label: Credit view
facts.text: Vestis is a leveraged but improving credit. Earnings and cash flow have recovered through fiscal 2026, and company-reported net leverage fell from 4.72x at October 3, 2025 to 4.10x at July 3, 2026, with liquidity of USD 351.8 million and no bank maturity before fiscal 2028. The strongest support is a recurring rental revenue base and USD 71.0 million of principal debt repaid since fiscal year end. The weakest point is that revenue and net volumes are still falling, so the recovery rests on a cost programme whose savings management, not the filings, has quantified. Two things decide the outcome: whether covenant EBITDA stays ahead of a maximum net leverage ratio that steps down from 5.00x to 4.75x and then 4.50x, and whether the receivables facility due August 2, 2027 is renewed or replaced.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Vestis has reduced reported leverage on every measure while its top line has contracted. Company-reported net leverage moved from 4.72x at October 3, 2025 to 4.83x at January 2, 2026, 4.47x at April 3, 2026 and 4.10x at July 3, 2026, and the leverage on the financial handoff's basis (company Adjusted EBITDA, principal debt plus finance leases) moved from 5.19x to 4.33x for total debt and from 5.07x to 4.13x for net debt over the same dates [CP-1, Chart data: leverage]. The mechanism is both a smaller numerator (principal debt of USD 1,097.5 million at July 3, 2026 after repayments) and a larger denominator, because trailing Adjusted EBITDA rose from USD 257,425 thousand to USD 290,437 thousand. For creditors this is genuine progress, categorised as Documentary Fact for the reported ratios and Analyst Interpretation for the reading that it reflects operations rather than only repayment.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The covenant cushion is adequate today and narrows on a known schedule. At July 3, 2026 the reported ratio of 4.10x sat 0.90x below the 5.00x maximum, equal to an EBITDA cushion of USD 52,961 thousand or 18.0% of covenant EBITDA; holding July 3, 2026 net debt constant, the same cushion falls to USD 40,272 thousand (13.7%) at 4.75x and USD 26,174 thousand (8.9%) at 4.50x [CP-1, Calculation steps]. Any shortfall in plan savings or a rise in net debt therefore bites first at the 4.50x test from the first quarter of fiscal 2027. The calculation is static and company-reported; it is not a forecast. The minimum interest cover covenant of 2.00x looks distant on an indicative basis (3.35x on covenant EBITDA over interest expense, net), but the executed definition is not supplied and the company does not print the ratio.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Business risk is moderate: the revenue base is recurring but shrinking. About 95% of fiscal 2025 revenue was recurring rental under multi-year contracts, spread over more than 300,000 accounts with the ten largest customers under 10% of revenue [CP-1A, Company and operating model]. Against that, nine month revenue fell 1.9%, net volumes fell 2.0%, partly through a deliberate exit of unprofitable business, and fiscal 2025 included the loss of a national account [CP-1, Financial base view; CP-1A, Credit translations]. The mechanism is operating leverage: with a fixed plant and route network, falling volume compresses margin unless cost is removed at least as fast, so the recovery in earnings depends on the transformation plan and on pricing, both of which management reports as working through the third quarter.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The transformation plan carries the earnings case and is mostly a management claim. Management targets annual savings of at least USD 75 million by the end of fiscal 2026 and reports roughly USD 30 million realised through the third quarter, while the estimated plan cost has risen from a range of USD 25 million to USD 30 million in the 10-K to a range of USD 35 million to USD 40 million in the latest 10-Q [CP-1A, Conflicts and inherited items]. Category: Management Language for the savings, Documentary Fact for the cost estimate change. For creditors the implication is that covenant headroom is partly a function of adjustments and savings that have not been independently verified, and execution risk includes service disruption and customer attrition.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Liquidity is adequate and bank maturities are distant. Liquidity of USD 351.8 million at July 3, 2026 comprised USD 294.2 million of revolver availability and USD 57.7 million of cash, with no revolver borrowings; the term loans mature in fiscal 2028 (USD 436.0 million) and fiscal 2031 (USD 661.5 million) [CP-1, Chart data: liquidity and debt maturities]. The revolver commitment of USD 300 million also matures in September 2028, so the first bank refinancing is just under two years away, not immediate.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The receivables securitization is the nearest funding event and a source of cash flow flattery. The USD 250 million facility is scheduled to terminate on August 2, 2027, and USD 212.3 million of receivables had been sold and derecognized at July 3, 2026, up USD 9.8 million since October 3, 2025 [CP-1, Calculation steps]. The mechanism is that the sold balance is not debt on the balance sheet; if the facility ended without replacement, receivables would return to the balance sheet and be funded from cash and the revolver, the credit agreement caps such facilities at USD 250 million, and the company's own net debt table does not include the sold balance. How the covenant counts the sold balance is unresolved: adding it to company net debt at July 3, 2026 gives 4.82x against the 5.00x maximum, and the same exercise at October 3, 2025 gives 5.45x, above the maximum then in force although the company reported compliance, which suggests the covenant does not count the whole balance on that basis. Category: Analyst Interpretation resting on an illustrative calculation, with the executed definition Not supplied.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Cash flow quality improved but should be read with care. Nine month operating cash flow was USD 160,873 thousand against USD 33,302 thousand a year earlier, and trailing twelve month free cash flow of USD 136,411 thousand was 47.0% of trailing Adjusted EBITDA [CP-1, Calculation steps]. Of the USD 127,571 thousand increase, the accepted financial handoff attributes USD 79.0 million to changes in operating assets and liabilities, while receivables sold rose by USD 9.8 million and USD 34,256 thousand of plan cash costs were absorbed in operating cash flow. Implication: free cash flow is real but includes working capital release that is unlikely to repeat at the same scale, and dividends and buybacks are restricted until conditions are met, so cash is going to debt service rather than shareholders.

facts.text: Governance looks creditor-neutral with monitoring items. facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Strengths. First, recurring revenue and breadth: recurring weekly rental is about 95% of revenue, with no meaningful customer concentration, which supports revenue visibility and limits event risk [Documentary Fact, from the business handoff]. Second, deleveraging with real cash generation: principal debt is down USD 71.0 million since October 3, 2025 and trailing free cash flow of USD 136,411 thousand funded it, with the revolver undrawn [Documentary Fact for the debt and cash flow, from the financial handoff]. Third, liquidity and maturity profile: liquidity of USD 351.8 million and no bank maturity until fiscal 2028 give time to execute the plan [Documentary Fact]. Fourth, a single secured bank facility with no junior debt in the sources: all funded borrowings sit in one credit agreement (finance leases and the receivables facility sit alongside it) guaranteed by the company and substantially all wholly-owned domestic material subsidiaries and secured on substantially all tangible assets, which keeps the structure simple and the covenant package, once read in full, central to monitoring [Documentary Fact; legal capacity Not supplied]. Fifth, improving margins: trailing Adjusted EBITDA margin was 10.8% against 9.4% for fiscal 2025 on the company's non-GAAP definition [Management Language, company-defined].

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Weaknesses. First, leverage remains high and the covenant tightens: reported net leverage of 4.10x is below the 5.00x maximum, but the maximum falls to 4.50x from the first quarter of fiscal 2027, which leaves a smaller cushion at constant net debt [Documentary Fact; Analyst Interpretation on the cushion]. Second, a shrinking top line: revenue down 1.9% and volume down 2.0% over nine months mean earnings recovery is cost-led [Documentary Fact]. Third, dependence on a management-quantified plan whose cost estimate has risen and whose savings are unaudited [Management Language]. Fourth, off-balance-sheet receivables funding with a defined end date and unresolved covenant treatment [Documentary Fact; Analyst Interpretation on the covenant]. Fifth, definition risk: two company figures for fiscal 2025 Adjusted EBITDA differ, and covenant EBITDA includes adjustments the company defines [Documentary Fact]. Sixth, leadership and legal overhang: an interim chief financial officer and pending securities class actions [Documentary Fact; exposure Insufficient Information]. Seventh, supply chain concentration: about 60% of uniforms and linens are made in two plants in Mexico, with tariff sensitivity not quantified [Documentary Fact; sensitivity Insufficient Information].

Source sufficiency is distinct from completion of downstream analysis.

The filings name no separate borrower, parent or sponsor in the context (the context leaves borrower, parent, guarantors and sponsor blank; blank is not zero). The Credit Agreement names Vestis Corporation as U.S. Borrower and Canadian Linen and Uniform Service Corp. as Canadian Borrower (10-K page:151, exhibit 10.5); guarantors are described in the debt note (10-K page:116).

Period note: the context names current period q2-2026 and prior period fy-2025. The pack also holds the fiscal third quarter 2026 filings (quarter ended July 3, 2026, filed August 11, 2026), which are later than the context's current period. Fiscal 2025 ended October 3, 2025 and was a 53-week year (Q3 release page:4, "additional operating week in fiscal 2025"). ## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| The seven sources cover the annual period and three quarters they name and can support all four downstream modules, with limitations. Debt, liquidity, covenant and operating evidence are located. | Medium | The executed credit agreement and its amendments are not supplied, so covenant terms rest on the company's own summaries. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Filed statements, notes and release reconciliations cover annual fiscal 2025 and the three quarters of fiscal 2026. | Debt, cash flow, liquidity and covenant work can rely on filed text rather than management claims. | High |

| Covenant terms and the company-reported leverage ratio come from summaries, and the receivables facility treatment in that ratio is unresolved. | Covenant headroom cannot be confirmed against the executed definitions. | Medium |
| The context names an earlier period than the latest filings, and nothing after August 11, 2026 is supplied. | Later events and the fiscal 2026 year-end are not covered. | Medium |
### Readiness view

Overall view: READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS. The effective source set is the three filed periodic reports for fiscal 2026, the filed annual report for fiscal 2025 and the three earnings releases that the company furnished with them. Together they give located statements, debt and covenant notes, liquidity tables and operating narrative for every consumer. The owner of each downstream method can perform its work, with bounded gaps that are listed below and carried into the consumer assessments. No source is blocked, no critical identity boundary is unresolved, and no source conflict was found between the filings and the releases on the figures checked for location. Source readiness here is not a statement that downstream analysis is complete, and no figure was normalized or reconciled in this module.

The strongest contrary evidence is that the governing financing documents are not in the pack: the Credit Agreement, its first and second amendments and the receivables facility documents are exhibits listed by reference only (10-K page:151 and page:152), so covenant levels, step-downs and definitions come from the company's own note and MD&A summaries. A second limitation is that the leverage ratio the company reports is its own non-GAAP presentation and the credit agreement definition, as summarized in the 10-Q, also counts advances under any receivables facility; how the receivables facility enters the reported ratio is not stated in the sources (see Version relationships and conflicts). Mechanism: when the executed definition cannot be read, headroom to the maintenance test depends on management's summary and its adjustments, so the consequence is that covenant headroom and any stress of it must be labelled as company-reported and unverified downstream.

What can proceed: financial extraction for fiscal 2025, the three fiscal 2026 quarters and the nine months ended July 3, 2026; debt, lease and receivables facility inventory; liquidity and cash flow; segment (United States and Canada) data; business, ownership-history and transformation narrative. What cannot proceed from this pack: any fact dated after August 11, 2026, any fiscal 2026 year-end result (the covenant schedule names a fiscal quarter ending October 2, 2026, which the pack does not report), ratings or market data (the context supplies none), the investor presentations that the releases mention, and verification of covenant definitions against executed documents. Next evidence action: obtain the executed Credit Agreement with both amendments and the receivables facility agreement; obtain any filing or release after August 11, 2026 and before the cutoff if one exists; obtain the investor presentations if slide-level evidence is needed.
### Source-by-source assessment

All seven sources are text extractions (JSONL pages of visible text). Extraction succeeded for every page, but a successful extraction is not a fidelity review: tables were flattened to text, and no image, chart or slide content is present or claimed. Filed statements control over releases; releases are management-attributed supporting material and carry non-GAAP measures.

### Version relationships and conflicts

- Periodic reports are separate, non-duplicate sources: each 10-Q covers a different quarter, and each release is a separate furnished exhibit for the same quarter as the 10-Q of the same date. None is a retained duplicate of another; none is collapsed. The later 10-Q restates balances as of the earlier fiscal year end (October 3, 2025) alongside current balances, so the 10-K and the Q3 10-Q both hold October 3, 2025 figures; downstream modules must cite the filing they use.

- Credit Agreement versions: the Q2 10-Q describes the original agreement, a first amendment (February 22, 2024) and a second amendment (May 1, 2025) and states the second amendment raised the maximum leverage ratio from 4.50x to step-down levels (Q2 10-Q page:20). The Q3 10-Q states the schedule that currently applies (page:20). The amendments themselves are not supplied. The first amendment is listed as an exhibit (10-K page:152); the executed text is not in the pack.

- Transformation plan cost estimate differs between sources by date, not by error: the 10-K subsequent events note estimates "range of $25 million to $30 million" (10-K page:147) and the Q3 10-Q estimates "range of $35 million to $40 million" (page:42). The later filing controls for current estimates; downstream modules must say which they use.

- Net leverage definition: the Q3 10-Q describes the covenant term as including advances under any receivables facility (page:52), while the Q3 release defines Net Debt as principal debt, letters of credit and finance lease obligations less cash (release page:10). Effect: the reported ratio may not equal the covenant ratio, and any covenant-headroom statement must say so. It is not resolved here.

## Findings
### Reader summary

### Financial base view

Vestis Corp entered fiscal 2026 with company-reported net leverage of 4.72x against a 5.25x maximum, and has since de-levered through earnings recovery and debt paydown rather than growth. Revenue is still falling: nine month revenue was $1,984.5 million, down 1.9% on the prior year, with net volumes down 2.0% and the decline attributed in part to a deliberate exit of unprofitable volume under the transformation plan (Q3 10-Q page:46). Earnings are recovering from cost action: nine month operating income rose from 46,790 to 80,605 (US$ thousands), while nine month SG&A fell 44.0 million, of which a 15 million bad debt charge in Q2 fiscal 2025 explains part (Q3 10-Q page:46). Company Adjusted EBITDA on a trailing twelve month basis rose from 257,425 at fiscal 2025 year end to 290,437 at July 3, 2026 (US$ thousands, release page:14).

Debt is entirely secured bank debt plus finance leases: term loan A-2 of 436,000 due September 2028 and term loan B-1 of 661,500 due February 2031 (US$ thousands), with the 300 million revolver undrawn. Principal debt fell by 71.0 million from fiscal 2025 year end to July 3, 2026 (calculated below). Cash interest paid on principal debt was 55.7 million for nine months against 64.7 million a year earlier (Q3 10-Q page:16), consistent with lower borrowings and a lower weighted-average rate of 6.23% against 6.80% (Q3 10-Q page:21).

On the metrics used for the charts below (company Adjusted EBITDA, principal debt plus finance leases), total debt over trailing EBITDA moved from 5.19x to 4.33x and net debt over trailing EBITDA from 5.07x to 4.13x between fiscal 2025 year end and July 3, 2026. The company's own covenant ratio, which uses covenant Adjusted EBITDA and adds letters of credit, moved from 4.72x to 4.10x against a maximum of 5.25x stepping to 5.00x (release page:16, Q3 10-Q page:20). Liquidity at July 3, 2026 was 351.8 million, made of 294.2 million of revolver availability and 57.7 million of cash.

Three issues keep the view at medium confidence. First, the executed credit agreement is not in the pack, so the covenant definition is read from summaries, and those summaries define covenant indebtedness to include advances under any receivables facility (Q3 10-Q page:52) while the company's net debt table has no such line (release page:16); the sold receivables balance was 212.3 million at July 3, 2026. Second, the maximum leverage ratio steps down to 4.75x for the quarter ending October 2, 2026 and 4.50x from the first quarter of fiscal 2027 (Q3 10-Q page:20), so today's headroom is not permanent. Third, the receivables facility is scheduled to terminate on August 2, 2027 (Q3 10-Q page:50); because the sold balance is off balance sheet, its end would draw on liquidity. The credit read-through is a deleveraging credit with adequate near-term liquidity and no bank maturity before fiscal 2028, but with a covenant test that tightens, definition risk around receivables, a shrinking top line and an earnings recovery driven by cost reductions and pricing while revenue and volume still decline.

### Calculation steps
- Principal debt reduction: 1,168,500 less 1,097,500 equals 71,000 (US$ thousands) between October 3, 2025 and July 3, 2026.

- Trailing cash interest paid on principal debt (US$ millions, printed to one decimal): FY2025 93.6. Q1: 93.6 + 20.1 - 23.2 = 90.5 (Q1 10-Q page:15). Q2: 93.6 + 38.3 - 43.8 = 88.1 (Q2 10-Q page:16). Q3: 93.6 + 55.7 - 64.7 = 84.6 (Q3 10-Q page:16).

- Covenant-style interest cover, indicative only: the covenant is Adjusted EBITDA over consolidated interest expense, minimum 2.00x (Q3 10-Q page:52). The company does not print the ratio. Covenant Adjusted EBITDA over interest expense, net: Q3 LTM 294,037 / 87,717 = 3.352 (3.35x); FY2025 277,825 / 92,264 = 3.011 (3.01x). The agreement's definition of consolidated interest expense is not supplied, so these are not compliance figures.

- Cover including receivables facility fees, mixed basis: securitization fees LTM 12,163 (release page:14). LTM Adjusted EBITDA adds these fees back, so charging them as a financing cost: 290.437 / (84.6 + 12.163) = 3.002 (3.00x). Cash interest is on a paid basis and the fees are on an expense basis.

- Operating cash flow change, nine months: 160,873 - 33,302 = 127,571. The 10-Q attributes 79.0 million (US$ millions) to changes in operating assets and liabilities (Q3 10-Q page:50). Receivables sold rose 212.3 - 202.5 = 9.8 million between October 3, 2025 and July 3, 2026. Cash paid for transformation costs and severance within nine month operating cash flow: 23,427 + 10,829 = 34,256 (release page:16).

- Static covenant sensitivity at July 3, 2026 balances (not a forecast): company Net Debt 1,205,382 divided by the next maxima. At 4.75x, EBITDA must be at least 1,205,382 / 4.75 = 253,765, a cushion of 294,037 - 253,765 = 40,272 (13.7%). At 4.50x, 1,205,382 / 4.50 = 267,863, a cushion of 26,174 (8.9%). The first applies to the quarter ending October 2, 2026 and the second from the first quarter of fiscal 2027 (Q3 10-Q page:20).

- Receivables facility sensitivity, illustrative: adding the 212.3 million sold balance to company Net Debt at July 3, 2026 gives (1,205,382 + 212,300) / 294,037 = 4.82x, against the 5.00x maximum. The same exercise for October 3, 2025 gives (1,310,875 + 202,500) / 277,825 = 5.45x, above the 5.25x maximum although the company reported compliance (10-K page:116). The covenant therefore evidently does not treat the whole sold balance as indebtedness, or its EBITDA differs; the executed definition is needed. These figures are not covenant measures.

- Liquidity: July 3, 2026 revolver availability 300,000 - 0 - 5,818 = 294,182; plus cash 57,659 = 351,841, equal to the company figure (release page:16). October 3, 2025: 300,000 - 26,000 - 5,818 = 268,182 (10-K prints 268.2); plus cash 29,748 = 297,930.
- Maturities: 436,000 + 661,500 = 1,097,500, equal to principal debt at July 3, 2026.

## Gaps
### Definition risks and conflicts

- Fiscal 2025 Adjusted EBITDA: the outlook tables in the Q2 and Q3 releases show fiscal 2025 actual Adjusted EBITDA of $272.6 million (Q3 release page:4), while the reconciliation shows 257,425 for the twelve months ended October 3, 2025 (release page:14). The difference, 272.6 less 257.425, is 15.175 million. No reconciliation of the two is in the text. This handoff uses 257,425 because it is reconciled to net income; the chart values for FY2025 would be lower in leverage terms if 272.6 were right (total debt / EBITDA 1,334.805 / 272.6 = 4.90x).
- Fiscal 2025 free cash flow: the same outlook table prints $5.9 million while operating cash flow less purchases is 5,769 (US$ thousands). Immaterial, unexplained.
- Covenant indebtedness includes advances under any receivables facility (Q3 10-Q page:52) but the company Net Debt table has no such line (release page:16). Unresolved; see the sensitivity above.

- The company ratio and the chart ratio differ in EBITDA (covenant versus Adjusted) and in letters of credit; neither is a verified covenant calculation because the executed agreement is not supplied.
- Fiscal 2025 had 53 weeks (10-K page:65); fiscal 2025 columns and the 12-month periods are not like-for-like.
- Plan cost estimate rose from 25 to 30 million (10-K page:147) to 35 to 40 million (Q3 10-Q page:42); cost recognised in nine months was 23.2 million consulting and 8.0 million severance.
### Items not supplied or not calculated
- Executed credit agreement, amendments and receivables facility documents: Not supplied (carried from the readiness handoff).
- Covenant interest coverage ratio actually reported by the company: Not supplied; the indicative figure above is calculated.
- Receivables facility availability or undrawn capacity: Not supplied; only the sold balance is stated. The facility is excluded from the liquidity chart.
- Quarterly LTM cost of services, SG&A, operating income and pre-tax income: Not printed; the cells say so rather than calculating from mismatched periods.
- Fiscal 2026 year-end (the fiscal quarter ending October 2, 2026) and anything after August 11, 2026: Not supplied.
- Pension withdrawal liability amount and litigation exposure: no amounts extracted.

- Segment detail (United States and Canada) was reviewed but is not tabulated in the required financial table; nine month reportable segment operating income was 141,525 for the United States and 6,457 for Canada on revenue of 1,802,551 and 181,937 (Q3 10-Q page:34).
- Pounds processed and revenue per pound are management estimates and are not in the filings (release page:12).
### Subsequent events

The pack holds no event after August 11, 2026. Within the fiscal third quarter, the company executed a long-term outsourcing arrangement for transactional support functions (Q3 10-Q page:42) and entered amended offer letters with its interim chief financial officer on June 12, 2026 (Q3 10-Q page:56). The release says the outsourcing is expected to generate approximately 10 million of annual SG&A savings from fiscal 2027 (release page:2).
## Next module

Proceed to the business and transaction context (CP-1A) with these carried limitations: covenant figures are company-reported and unverified against executed documents; the receivables facility treatment and its August 2, 2027 termination date; the maximum leverage steps (4.75x, then 4.50x); the dividend and buyback restriction until the earlier of a compliant quarter ending after October 2, 2026 or two consecutive quarters at or below 4.50x (Q3 10-Q page:20); the conflict between two fiscal 2025 Adjusted EBITDA figures; and the 53-week fiscal 2025. Later modules should cite figures from this handoff by period label and should state that Q3 FY2026 is the latest period although the context names Q2 FY2026.

### Business and transaction view

Vestis is a standalone, publicly listed provider of uniform rental and workplace supplies in the United States and Canada, created by the spin-off from Aramark on September 30, 2023. The sources disclose no sponsor, and no parent or borrower distinct from the listed registrant is named in them; they show no leveraged buyout, acquisition or dividend recapitalisation in the period examined. The one transaction that defines the capital structure is the separation itself: the company borrowed under a new senior secured credit agreement and transferred roughly 1,457 million (US$) of proceeds to Aramark (10-K page:112). Since then the only financing changes are a refinancing of one term loan in February 2024, a covenant amendment in May 2025 that traded relief for restrictions on dividends, buybacks and receivables facilities, and a receivables securitization put in place in August 2024.

The operating model gives good revenue visibility: recurring weekly rental service under multi-year contracts is 95% of revenue, more than 300,000 accounts and no meaningful concentration (the ten largest customers are under 10% of revenue). The countervailing evidence is that revenue is nonetheless contracting: the nine-month decline in revenue and the quarter's lower volume are explained in part by a deliberate exit of unprofitable business under the transformation plan, and fiscal 2025 revenue included the loss of a national account customer. The mechanism matters for creditors: a recurring base protects against sudden revenue loss, but contract exit costs are modest relative to a service-quality failure, and the business has a high fixed cost base of plants and routes, so volume decline compresses operating leverage unless cost is removed at the same pace. This is why the earlier financial handoff shows earnings recovery driven by cost reduction and pricing rather than volume.

The credit-relevant change is the transformation plan launched in the first quarter of fiscal 2026. Management targets annual cost savings of at least $75 million by the end of fiscal 2026 and has roughly $30 million realised through the third quarter (Q3 release page:2). These are management claims, not filed facts; the filed fact is that third-party consulting and severance costs have been incurred and that the estimated plan cost has been raised since the 10-K. Governance signals are mixed rather than adverse: no extraction-oriented behaviour is documented, dividends are suspended by the credit agreement amendment, but the principal financial officer role is filled on an interim basis and securities class actions allege misleading statements about pricing practices and outlook (allegations, not findings). Evidence quality is High for filed facts and Low for management claims on savings and market position.

### Reader summary

Delivery of plan savings decides the outcome. | Medium | Covenant terms are company summaries, the receivables facility treatment is unresolved and the executed credit documents are not supplied. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Reported net leverage fell from 4.72x to 4.10x between October 3, 2025 and July 3, 2026 as debt was repaid and earnings recovered. | Covenant cushion widened to 0.90x, but it narrows as the maximum steps down to 4.75x and then 4.50x. | Medium |

| Operating cash flow rose sharply in the nine months, helped by working capital and higher receivables sales. | Part of the improvement may not repeat, so free cash flow quality needs monitoring. | Medium |

### Credit view

Vestis is a leveraged but improving credit. Earnings and cash flow have recovered through fiscal 2026, and company-reported net leverage fell from 4.72x at October 3, 2025 to 4.10x at July 3, 2026, with liquidity of USD 351.8 million and no bank maturity before fiscal 2028. The strongest support is a recurring rental revenue base and USD 71.0 million of principal debt repaid since fiscal year end. The weakest point is that revenue and net volumes are still falling, so the recovery rests on a cost programme whose savings management, not the filings, has quantified. Two things decide the outcome: whether covenant EBITDA stays ahead of a maximum net leverage ratio that steps down from 5.00x to 4.75x and then 4.50x, and whether the receivables facility due August 2, 2027 is renewed or replaced.
### Key findings

Vestis has reduced reported leverage on every measure while its top line has contracted. Company-reported net leverage moved from 4.72x at October 3, 2025 to 4.83x at January 2, 2026, 4.47x at April 3, 2026 and 4.10x at July 3, 2026, and the leverage on the financial handoff's basis (company Adjusted EBITDA, principal debt plus finance leases) moved from 5.19x to 4.33x for total debt and from 5.07x to 4.13x for net debt over the same dates [CP-1, Chart data: leverage]. The mechanism is both a smaller numerator (principal debt of USD 1,097.5 million at July 3, 2026 after repayments) and a larger denominator, because trailing Adjusted EBITDA rose from USD 257,425 thousand to USD 290,437 thousand. For creditors this is genuine progress, categorised as Documentary Fact for the reported ratios and Analyst Interpretation for the reading that it reflects operations rather than only repayment.

The covenant cushion is adequate today and narrows on a known schedule. At July 3, 2026 the reported ratio of 4.10x sat 0.90x below the 5.00x maximum, equal to an EBITDA cushion of USD 52,961 thousand or 18.0% of covenant EBITDA; holding July 3, 2026 net debt constant, the same cushion falls to USD 40,272 thousand (13.7%) at 4.75x and USD 26,174 thousand (8.9%) at 4.50x [CP-1, Calculation steps]. Any shortfall in plan savings or a rise in net debt therefore bites first at the 4.50x test from the first quarter of fiscal 2027. The calculation is static and company-reported; it is not a forecast. The minimum interest cover covenant of 2.00x looks distant on an indicative basis (3.35x on covenant EBITDA over interest expense, net), but the executed definition is not supplied and the company does not print the ratio.

Business risk is moderate: the revenue base is recurring but shrinking. About 95% of fiscal 2025 revenue was recurring rental under multi-year contracts, spread over more than 300,000 accounts with the ten largest customers under 10% of revenue [CP-1A, Company and operating model]. Against that, nine month revenue fell 1.9%, net volumes fell 2.0%, partly through a deliberate exit of unprofitable business, and fiscal 2025 included the loss of a national account [CP-1, Financial base view; CP-1A, Credit translations]. The mechanism is operating leverage: with a fixed plant and route network, falling volume compresses margin unless cost is removed at least as fast, so the recovery in earnings depends on the transformation plan and on pricing, both of which management reports as working through the third quarter.

The transformation plan carries the earnings case and is mostly a management claim. Management targets annual savings of at least USD 75 million by the end of fiscal 2026 and reports roughly USD 30 million realised through the third quarter, while the estimated plan cost has risen from a range of USD 25 million to USD 30 million in the 10-K to a range of USD 35 million to USD 40 million in the latest 10-Q [CP-1A, Conflicts and inherited items]. Category: Management Language for the savings, Documentary Fact for the cost estimate change. For creditors the implication is that covenant headroom is partly a function of adjustments and savings that have not been independently verified, and execution risk includes service disruption and customer attrition.

Liquidity is adequate and bank maturities are distant. Liquidity of USD 351.8 million at July 3, 2026 comprised USD 294.2 million of revolver availability and USD 57.7 million of cash, with no revolver borrowings; the term loans mature in fiscal 2028 (USD 436.0 million) and fiscal 2031 (USD 661.5 million) [CP-1, Chart data: liquidity and debt maturities]. The revolver commitment of USD 300 million also matures in September 2028, so the first bank refinancing is just under two years away, not immediate.

The receivables securitization is the nearest funding event and a source of cash flow flattery. The USD 250 million facility is scheduled to terminate on August 2, 2027, and USD 212.3 million of receivables had been sold and derecognized at July 3, 2026, up USD 9.8 million since October 3, 2025 [CP-1, Calculation steps]. The mechanism is that the sold balance is not debt on the balance sheet; if the facility ended without replacement, receivables would return to the balance sheet and be funded from cash and the revolver, the credit agreement caps such facilities at USD 250 million, and the company's own net debt table does not include the sold balance. How the covenant counts the sold balance is unresolved: adding it to company net debt at July 3, 2026 gives 4.82x against the 5.00x maximum, and the same exercise at October 3, 2025 gives 5.45x, above the maximum then in force although the company reported compliance, which suggests the covenant does not count the whole balance on that basis. Category: Analyst Interpretation resting on an illustrative calculation, with the executed definition Not supplied.

Cash flow quality improved but should be read with care. Nine month operating cash flow was USD 160,873 thousand against USD 33,302 thousand a year earlier, and trailing twelve month free cash flow of USD 136,411 thousand was 47.0% of trailing Adjusted EBITDA [CP-1, Calculation steps]. Of the USD 127,571 thousand increase, the accepted financial handoff attributes USD 79.0 million to changes in operating assets and liabilities, while receivables sold rose by USD 9.8 million and USD 34,256 thousand of plan cash costs were absorbed in operating cash flow. Implication: free cash flow is real but includes working capital release that is unlikely to repeat at the same scale, and dividends and buybacks are restricted until conditions are met, so cash is going to debt service rather than shareholders.

Governance looks creditor-neutral with monitoring items. No sponsor, dividend recapitalisation or creditor-adverse action is documented, dividends are restricted, and the company reports its covenant ratio and liquidity each quarter; offsetting this, the chief financial officer role is interim, securities class actions alleging misleading disclosure are in discovery, and tax-free spin-off restrictions and indemnification obligations to Aramark remain unquantified [CP-1A, Governance and sponsor behaviour]. Category: Documentary Fact for the events, Insufficient Information for the exposures.
### Strengths and weaknesses

Strengths. First, recurring revenue and breadth: recurring weekly rental is about 95% of revenue, with no meaningful customer concentration, which supports revenue visibility and limits event risk [Documentary Fact, from the business handoff]. Second, deleveraging with real cash generation: principal debt is down USD 71.0 million since October 3, 2025 and trailing free cash flow of USD 136,411 thousand funded it, with the revolver undrawn [Documentary Fact for the debt and cash flow, from the financial handoff]. Third, liquidity and maturity profile: liquidity of USD 351.8 million and no bank maturity until fiscal 2028 give time to execute the plan [Documentary Fact]. Fourth, a single secured bank facility with no junior debt in the sources: all funded borrowings sit in one credit agreement (finance leases and the receivables facility sit alongside it) guaranteed by the company and substantially all wholly-owned domestic material subsidiaries and secured on substantially all tangible assets, which keeps the structure simple and the covenant package, once read in full, central to monitoring [Documentary Fact; legal capacity Not supplied]. Fifth, improving margins: trailing Adjusted EBITDA margin was 10.8% against 9.4% for fiscal 2025 on the company's non-GAAP definition [Management Language, company-defined].

Weaknesses. First, leverage remains high and the covenant tightens: reported net leverage of 4.10x is below the 5.00x maximum, but the maximum falls to 4.50x from the first quarter of fiscal 2027, which leaves a smaller cushion at constant net debt [Documentary Fact; Analyst Interpretation on the cushion]. Second, a shrinking top line: revenue down 1.9% and volume down 2.0% over nine months mean earnings recovery is cost-led [Documentary Fact]. Third, dependence on a management-quantified plan whose cost estimate has risen and whose savings are unaudited [Management Language]. Fourth, off-balance-sheet receivables funding with a defined end date and unresolved covenant treatment [Documentary Fact; Analyst Interpretation on the covenant]. Fifth, definition risk: two company figures for fiscal 2025 Adjusted EBITDA differ, and covenant EBITDA includes adjustments the company defines [Documentary Fact]. Sixth, leadership and legal overhang: an interim chief financial officer and pending securities class actions [Documentary Fact; exposure Insufficient Information]. Seventh, supply chain concentration: about 60% of uniforms and linens are made in two plants in Mexico, with tariff sensitivity not quantified [Documentary Fact; sensitivity Insufficient Information].

No new calculation is made in this module. Every figure is taken from the accepted financial handoff by its period label, and the ratios, cushions and sensitivities cited were calculated there from the filed inputs shown in that handoff.

## Calculations
Recomputations performed in this review, all from figures printed in the sources or in the reports (US$ unless stated):

- Fourth quarter length of fiscal 2025: quarter ends June 27, 2025 and October 3, 2025 are 98 days apart, which is 14 weeks; the other quarters tested (September 27, 2024 to December 27, 2024, and October 3, 2025 to January 2, 2026) are 91 days, or 13 weeks. Every trailing window ending at October 3, 2025, January 2, 2026, April 3, 2026 and July 3, 2026 contains that 98-day quarter.

- Indicative extra-week EBITDA: 51.6 million of revenue less 37.9 million of cost of services less 7.2 million of SG&A equals 6.5 million (S1 page:68). This is a reviewer estimate from the company's own exclusion figures, not a disclosed EBITDA.

- Indicative effect at July 3, 2026: chart net debt over EBITDA is 1,199.564 / (290.437 - 6.5) = 4.22x against 4.13x; company ratio is 1,205.382 / (294.037 - 6.5) = 4.19x against 4.10x; cushion to the 5.00x maximum is 294.037 - 6.5 - 1,205.382 / 5.00 = 46.5 million against 53.0 million (US$ millions). The 5.00x test is passed either way, so the finding is Material, not Critical.
- Recomputation of the financial handoff's ratios, cushions, free cash flow, trailing cash interest and sensitivities matched the stated values to the stated rounding in every case (register above).
- Cross-module identity: every figure in the synthesis was found in the financial or business handoff with the same value, unit and period.
